articles.title: Inflation under Trump is only about half the rate under Biden. Voters are still just as mad.
articles.summary: So far in President Trump's second term, prices in the US have risen only about half as quickly compared to his predecessor's four years in office. Yet Trump has a 72% disapproval rating on the issue and risks paying a steep political price — just as former President Joe Biden did — with voters drawing a direct connection between rising prices and the president's policies. In the last election cycle, prices of all items rose more than 20% during Biden's term , sparking widespread voter angst. This time around, price growth is notably slower, rising 5.4% in a little less than two years since Inauguration Day. But a Yahoo Finance analysis of price data shows that a few major outliers have hit Americans' wallets in an outsized way, largely due to increases in goods affected by the war in Iran and tariffs. Fuel oil and gasoline are perhaps the most dramatic examples, spiking over 30% beginning in March in response to the war in Iran and the closing of the Strait of Hormuz. And voters have noticed, as evidenced in poll after poll. A New York Times/Siena poll released this week found 73% of likely voters disapprove of the president's handling of gas prices. Trump underscored the salience of energy prices when he posted a charge this week that "Iran is doing everything they can to drive up the price of Oil prior to the US Midterm Election." Trump has often pushed back against questions about high energy prices, saying they won't be a problem once the Iran war ends. Read more: How oil price shocks ripple through your wallet, from gas to groceries Link between price spikes and Trump policies The connection between price increases and Trump's tariff policy has also been in evidence. Coffee prices have risen nearly 23% during Trump's second term (more than double the rate under Biden) as tariffs raised prices before Trump scrapped many of the coffee duties late last year in response to coffee drinkers' unhappiness. Goods like toys and footwear have likewise risen rapidly as importers from China and elsewhere in Asia faced new tariffs. Toys are a particularly stark example, falling by 4.6% during Biden's term and then rising by 7.8% so far in Trump's term. "Maybe the children will have two dolls instead of 30 dolls, and maybe the two dolls will cost a couple of bucks more than they would normally," Trump said in a rare acknowledgment of tariff-fueled price increases when he was pressed on the issue in April. Other goods have moved in the opposite direction. Eggs jumped by an average of 2.57% each month when Biden was in the White House, but have dropped 3.82% each month of Trump's term so far, the analysis shows. But tariffs remain in focus and unpopular, with an average of polls from the Silver Bulletin finding that 62.7% of Americans disapprove of how Trump has handled trade and tariffs versus 32.8% who approve. President Donald Trump is seen after a rally on October 22 in Sioux City, Iowa.. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images) Anna Moneymaker via Getty Images Gas in focus in the final weeks of the campaign Despite the different roots, inflation has emerged as the central political problem for Trump and his party — as it was for Biden and Democrats — and comes as early voting is already underway for the Nov. 3 midterms. And perhaps no individual price tag is more politically charged, for any president, than the cost of a gallon of gas. Trump is trying to make his case as gas prices are averaging about $4.30 per gallon and diesel is elevated after setting an all-time price record last month, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA). Trump has taken multiple actions just this week to try to rein in prices, including $8 billion in support for farmers and invoking the Defense Production Act on Thursday to direct new funds to increase refining capacity. Yahoo Finance Trump touted the moves before voters in Iowa on Thursday , saying the release of $150 million would lead to more production of diesel and gasoline. Yet he faces the inconvenient fact that his record on gas prices is now all but indistinguishable from Biden's. Since Jan. 20, 2025, prices have averaged $3.449 per gallon according to data from the Energy Information Administration . Under Biden, the average price was $3.455 per gallon over his four years. Trump spent much of the last campaign promising the opposite, pledging $ 2 per gallon gasoline and vanishing inflation in nearly every 2024 campaign speech. That is leading voters to blame the president for the state of affairs. This week's national poll from the New York Times and Siena University found that 75% of voters view economic conditions as only fair or poor, and a solid majority put the blame on Trump. As Ipsos also put it this week in a summary of recent findings :  "Americans' confidence in the economy has been bad since the Iran war began [and] now the bottom has dropped out." Ben Werschkul is a Washington correspondent for Yahoo Finance. articles.title: Trump announces $4 billion Audi factory in Georgia ahead of midterms
articles.summary: By Bo Erickson and David Shepardson PERRY, Georgia, Oct 25 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump announced on Saturday that Audi plans to build a $4 billion assembly plant in Georgia that will produce 200,000 SUVs annually, as he seeks to convince Americans to back Republicans in the November midterm elections. Trump, who has pressured automakers ‌to move production to the United States and has raised tariffs on autos, steel, aluminum and parts, made the announcement at a rally in Perry, near Macon in ‌central Georgia, where Volkswagen's premium subsidiary intends to build its first US assembly plant. Last year, Trump's tariffs dealt Audi a €1.2 billion ($1.4 billion) blow as it imports all its vehicles for the US market from Europe or Mexico. Georgia has ​competitive election races for US Senate and governor and Trump is eager to make the case that his auto tariffs are helping the US economy. Critics say they have boosted vehicle prices and that the trade uncertainty has delayed some automaker investments. "We are planning to bring our biggest and most premium SUVs, and produce them here in Macon, Georgia," Audi CEO Gernot Doellner said at the event. "This is a long-term investment because we believe in the American market." In Germany, meanwhile, there has been increasing tension between Volkswagen management and workers over massive job cuts in the carmaker's home market, including ‌possible plant closures in light of rising costs and stiff Asian ⁠competition. "It is right and necessary to better tap into the US market via a new plant," said Christiane Benner, head of the IG Metall union and Volkswagen's deputy supervisory board chair. "However, firm prospects for workers at all sites, particularly those here in Germany, must be clearly defined and set ⁠out." She said a final decision on the investment would have to be taken by Volkswagen's supervisory board. Olaf Lies, state premier of the German state of Lower Saxony, Volkswagen's second-largest shareholder, said that expanded production in the US was an opportunity provided German workers also benefit. "Growth in America must secure jobs and value creation here and must not displace them," he said. REPUBLICAN SAYS TARIFFS BROUGHT AUDI PLANT TO UNITED STATES Audi said ​the ​investment will create approximately 4,500 jobs. Construction is scheduled to begin next year, with production starting in the ​early 2030s, Audi said. The plant is expected to assemble the Audi Q7, ‌Q8 and Q9 SUVs, a US official told Reuters. Audi also plans to build 25,000 vehicles a year in neighboring South Carolina, the official said. Some of the vehicles, now built in Europe, would be exported, the official added. Those vehicles will be assembled at a $2 billion plant of VW's off-road brand Scout Motors that is under construction in Blythewood, near the state capital, Columbia, the official said. "We regard the region as a key market for profitable growth," Volkswagen CEO Oliver Blume said. "A potential Audi plant in the US would create further conditions for this." Trump has cut government incentives for electric vehicles, causing a significant reduction in EV and battery production in the country. US vehicle and parts employment has fallen since Trump took office last year. A gold ‌Audi with manufacturer license plates was parked outside Trump's rally. US Senator Bernie Moreno, an Ohio Republican, said ​late on Saturday that "with this investment, Audi will build all of their SUVs exclusively in the US". He said ​the Audi plant "would never have happened without tariffs, without common sense regulations and without ​eliminating California’s ability to regulate fuel economy standards". Audi sales have fallen for two consecutive years and slid 7% in the first half of 2026 as ‌fierce competition in China and US tariffs hit demand. Audi's US sales ​are down 16% this year. Audi's Neckarsulm plant in ​southwest Germany is one of four German Volkswagen plants facing possible closure after 2030. In July, Japan's Toyota said it would spend $3.6 billion to build a 2.5 million square foot (232,000 square metre) truck assembly line on its manufacturing campus in San Antonio, Texas, and shift some truck production to the US from Mexico. The Japanese automaker said the ​expansion would be completed by 2030, creating 2,000 jobs. Honda Motor is ‌considering building a US assembly plant but has warned it may not unless the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement on trade is extended. South Korea's Hyundai said last year that ​if it had certainty about USMCA, it "would immediately unlock over $20 billion in new American investments". (Reporting by Bo Erickson in Perry and David Shepardson in Washington; Additional ​reporting by Christoph Steitz and Rachel More; Editing by Nia Williams, Rod Nickel and David Goodman) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://finance.yahoo.com/news/trump-set-announce-plan-audi-213133434.html

articles.title: Economic pressures put new Midwestern states in play for the midterms
articles.summary: Supporters listen as Democratic US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed speaks at a rally at Wayne State University in Detroit on October 22. - Jeff Kowalsky/AFP/Getty Images Democrats could be poised for a revival in the heartland, as furor over high costs and doubt about President Donald Trump’s willingness to change the nation’s trajectory threaten to loosen the GOP’s grip on working-class voters. A decade after the Trump era began, when he first turned Midwestern political battlegrounds into reliably Republican states, the fallout from policies of his second term have rippled through the agriculture sector and broader economies across the Great Plains and the Rust Belt. Iowa and Ohio, which have not been competitive since former President Barack Obama was on the ballot, are in play. And ruby-red states like Kansas, Nebraska and Indiana are not exempt. The shift is happening up and down the ballot, with tight contests for the House, Senate and governor blanketing the middle of the country. From spring planting to fall harvest, anxiety over Trump’s war with Iran and the fallout from his trade battles has turned into alarm. In conversations across the region, voters point to the soaring cost of gas and diesel , as well as high grocery prices and interest rates. A whipsaw tariff policy has forced farmers to pay more for fertilizer, while some manufacturers, footing higher bills for imported components, have laid off workers. Trump’s decision to allow imported beef has infuriated ranchers. And spending cuts targeting healthcare and grant programs have caused further strain. Promises to revitalize the nation’s manufacturing sector remain unfulfilled. And even before the Iran war sent costs soaring, several of these battleground states were in fiscal decline. Iowa, for example, recorded the weakest annual growth rate in the country in 2025, according to the federal Bureau of Economic Analysis, a searing indictment for Republicans who have had control of state government for more than a decade. “I think everybody in agriculture is tired, would be the best way to put it. They’re just tired,” Steve Kuiper, a farmer and president of the Iowa Corn Growers Association, told CNN. “They feel very beat up right now, demoralized.” It has all fueled a hunger for change — and created an opening for Democratic candidates. “A lot of the promises the president made to bring costs down, to not start new foreign wars, to deliver on his economic message, have not come to fruition,” said Beau Bayh, the third-generation scion of Indiana’s most famous Democratic political family. If he wins his race for secretary of state, he’d be the first member of his party to win statewide in Indiana in 14 years. Trump knows better than most presidents that midterm elections are a reflection — and referendum — on the party in power. He experienced it in 2018, when Republicans held control of the Senate but lost their majority in the House — including three seats in Iowa. GOP officials tell CNN they fear a repeat of that scenario. The US Capitol building seen on October 1 in Washington, DC. - Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images The travel plans of both parties tell the tale, with Trump set to visit Michigan on Sunday after making stops in Ohio, Kansas, Nebraska and Iowa in a monthlong campaign blitz. Obama traveled to Michigan and Ohio on Saturday, rallying support in two states he once won. Polls suggest voters are willing to punish the Republicans in power in Washington, even though they also hold dim views of the Democratic brand. “It’s not that they’ve been overwhelmed by the Democratic Party, it’s just that they’re really, really pissed off,” Tom Vilsack, a Democratic former Iowa governor, told CNN. “They want to send a message of disappointment. When you’re upset with someone, you want to find a way to send a message. You don’t swallow it, you send that message.” Vilsack, who served two terms as agriculture secretary in the Obama administration, said economic frustrations across the agriculture and manufacturing sectors have been rising long before the Trump era. But he said the promises Trump made during his three campaigns, particularly when he pledged to bring prices down only two years ago, are feeding the anger. “He builds up the hope that it’s going to be fundamentally different,” Vilsack said. “That was interpreted that he’s going to bring back the good times. He failed to do that.” Former Minnesota Gov. Tim Pawlenty, who was the last Republican to win that office in his reelection two decades ago, said Trump would be better off talking about rising costs and how he intends to change course. “It’s going to be a blue wave,” Pawlenty told CNN. “We just don’t know if it’s knee-deep, waist-deep, or going to hit us right in the face.” The House is all but certain to fall from GOP control, he said, but added: “The real chance for Republicans to salvage something out of this is to hang on to the Senate and that’s a real possibility.” House and Senate in the balance In Iowa and Ohio, Democrats have a shot at winning Senate races that are crucial to the net four-seat gain they need to claim a majority — a goal that eluded them in 2018. Their odds look even better in those states’ governor’s races, potentially giving the party a foothold in statehouses where Republicans have trifectas: control of the executive, legislative and judicial branches. But the Democratic revival could extend even further. Megachurch pastor Adam Hamilton has the GOP scrambling to save the seat of Sen. Roger Marshall in Kansas . An independent candidate, Dan Osborn, has rallied Democratic support and thrown a curveball into Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts’ bid for a second term in Nebraska. And a slew of House seats across the Midwest held by Republicans are in play. Democrats believe they could win as many as three GOP-held seats each in Iowa and Ohio, plus potentially four more in Michigan. The party is also targeting an Omaha-based district in Nebraska and one in southeastern Wisconsin’s Driftless Area. If the election breaks in Democrats’ favor in a big way, another House seat in Nebraska, as well as one seat each in Indiana and Kansas, could also prove to be much more competitive than either party expected early in the 2026 election cycle. Republicans aren’t conceding any of those races. And they believe they have Democrats on defense in the Upper Midwest — particularly Michigan, where progressive former public health official Abdul El-Sayed is locked in an expensive and bitter Senate race against Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers. unknown content item - Speaking in Sioux City, Iowa, on Thursday, Trump urged voters to pretend he was on the ballot and vote to ensure a “booming Iowa economy.” “If you get out and vote like you did in 2024, we win in a landslide, you know, we win in a landslide,” he said Even as the president boasts of America’s golden age, with an economy envied by the world, he also makes clear he understands the challenges people are facing. At most every stop along the way of his red-state October blitz, he has offered sweeteners to voters if they stick with Republican candidates. From $8 billion in new aid to farmers announced in Kansas to promises of building the nation’s largest steel plant in eastern Iowa to a commitment he made in Nebraska to temporarily ease diesel costs, Trump has made a series of pledges that follow his offer of giving every adult American $5,000 if Republicans retain their grip on Washington. The promises are barely even repeated by GOP candidates, who know they ring hollow with many voters. Democrats acknowledge the uphill climb for winning all of the narrowly divided Senate races across the Midwest, particularly given their own brand and favorability challenges. But Republican officials wonder whether Trump’s extensive travels to many of these states will backfire on down-ballot races. “When our leader, the president himself, does things that make me cringe, that’s difficult to tell people to vote for me,” said Jim Howell, a Republican member of the Sedgwick County Board of Commissioners in Wichita, who is also on the November ballot. “I really wish we had leaders that don’t make us cringe, but help us consider a way to come together.” Trump’s closing message A question hanging over the final week of the race is whether Trump’s relentless campaigning has awakened Republican voters to rally to his aid one last time in hopes of closing an enthusiasm gap. Iowa could be a place to watch, given Trump’s long history of winning there and his decision to hold two rallies in opposite corners of the state in the homestretch. But the president’s approach, a little more than one week from Election Day, has been to double down on the policies that have led many voters to sour on his second term. In Trump’s Sunday trip to Michigan, he’ll hold a rally at Port Huron — on the Canadian border. It will put on display his tariff battle with the United States’ northern neighbor, even though the party’s Senate nominee, former Rep. Mike Rogers, has attempted to break with Trump over the tariffs. “Here in Michigan, we know that Canada is not our enemy. We need to end this tariff war — now,” Rogers said in a television ad his campaign launched this month. The GOP’s best hope might be to lean into the cultural battles that have helped them win over White, rural, working-class voters in recent elections. In Michigan, both Trump and Rogers have attempted to brand the Democratic nominee, El-Sayed, as supportive of extremist Islamist interests. But Democrats are fighting back. El-Sayed in recent days began airing an ad that features clips of Republicans and conservative media figures, including Fox News hosts, saying nice or helpful things about him and his campaign. Before those clips play, he lists issues where he suggests common cause with some in the MAGA movement, such as releasing the Jeffrey Epstein files and combatting Washington corruption. Ohio is another headache for Republicans. The party’s nominee for governor, Vivek Ramaswamy, faced sharp criticism from the man he is running to replace, two-term GOP Gov. Mike DeWine, for airing a controversial advertisement featuring the mother of his Democratic opponent, Amy Acton. Gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, alongside US President Donald Trump, speaks in Youngstown, Ohio, on October 12. - Kevin Lamarque/Reuters Both Ramaswamy and the president have dug in, defending the ad — and in doing so have turned the race into a test of whether voters will accept Trumpian tactics from candidates who are not Trump. And what’s receded from the forefront is the issue Ohio voters who spoke with CNN in recent days — including Republicans who support Ramaswamy — said is responsible for the state’s sudden competitiveness: the cost of living. “We all have to get gas. I have to go get gas right now in my car, and that’s difficult,” said Sheri Vorherr, a 55-year-old mother of five from Loveland who volunteered at a Ramaswamy rally in Cincinnati on Wednesday. She said she helps her oldest daughter buy groceries each week and sees the economic pinch brought on by inflation. “I don’t think it’s an easy fix. I think it’s things that are going to take time,” she said. “I do believe Trump is trying to do that — it’s just taking a lot longer.” CNN’s Phil Mattingly contributed to this report. articles.title: Amy Acton urges Trump and Vance to 'look at the facts' after Ramaswamy attack ad
articles.summary: Ohio Democratic gubernatorial nominee Amy Acton told ABC News in an interview Saturday that she hopes President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance will "look at the facts" of the abuse she says she endured as a child after they defended an attack ad made by GOP nominee Vivek Ramaswamy's campaign. Bipartisan backlash has hit Ramaswamy's campaign, after the release of the ad featuring Acton's estranged mother who Acton says stood by the man who was criminally charged with sexually abusing her as a child. Acton said she hasn't seen her mother since she was 12 years old. In the ad, Acton's mother, Donna Arthur, said Acton has lied about her past, though it doesn't mention the allegations of sexual abuse. Sue Ogrocki/AP Photo - PHOTO: Amy Acton In response to Trump and Vance who have doubled down on and defended the ad, Acton told ABC News, "My job is to work with anyone on any side of the aisle to solve problems instead of making them, and I would say I do hope they would look at the facts." Acton spoke to ABC News after a rally in Cleveland with former President Barack Obama. Trump doubles down on Amy Acton criticism as Ramaswamy ad controversy swirls Acton has alleged her mother's second husband molested her between the ages of 9 and 12. Charges were filed against her stepfather, and Acton testified against him. He pleaded not guilty, but fled the state before trial and never appeared before a judge. He died in 2004. Shannon Stapleton/Reuters - PHOTO: Ohio Midterm Elections Acton said she and her brother endured "extreme child abuse and neglect" in their childhood. "We were frequent flyers in children's services ... There are facts in this case: a grand jury indictment, fugitive out against bail, and that behavior went on and on," Acton said. Speaking to reporters this week about the ad, Trump dismissed questions about the allegations of Acton's sexual abuse, asserting at multiple points that the ad has "nothing to do" with Acton's stepfather. Spencer Platt/Getty Images - PHOTO: Ohio Republican Candidates Campaign At The Circleville Pumpkin Show Rally Similarly, Vance told rally attendees in Ohio earlier this week that he is "a little bit disgusted when I see Republicans across the country who are whining more about that advertisement than they are about what the congressional Democrats and other Democrats want to do to the United States of America." GOP Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine, who on Thursday told reporters in Columbus, Ohio, that the ad is "deeply, deeply troubling" and that the Ramaswamy campaign "needs to take it down," but he did not withdraw his endorsement of Ramaswamy. Asked whether she was disappointed that DeWine didn't withdraw his endorsement, Acton said it was "an honor and a privilege" to work with him during COVID-19 pandemic as the director of the Ohio Department of Health. Vance praises Ramaswamy for having 'audacity' to run controversial Amy Acton ad "I really do appreciate him calling out the facts of the case," Acton said. "That this was an indictment he knows better than others. He's a prosecutor. He started his career prosecuting cases like this, and he knew more than anyone. He knows who I am and knows my story." Speaking to reporters on Friday, Ramaswamy said the ad had nothing to do with childhood abuse. "We ran an ad about lying," he said. "Amy Acton is lying. She has been lying this entire campaign about me, about her record, about her history in this state." In a statement to ABC News, Connie Luck, a spokesperson for Ramaswamy said: "Ohioans can't afford a liberal governor who shows up for Obama but never shows up for them." Ramaswamy and Acton have never met in person. Asked what she would say to him, Acton said: "I really have no words for Mr. Ramaswamy. I think there is no low that he wouldn't sink to." Speaking to survivors of abuse, Acton said: "For those out there going through it now, hold on, please. If there's someone you feel safe with, say something about it." Obama blasts Trump, says Ramaswamy 'thirsty' for attention Acton campaigned Saturday alongside former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown, who's running to win back his seat, and Obama, who was the last Democratic presidential candidate to win the state of Ohio in a presidential election in 2012. Sue Ogrocki/AP Photo - PHOTO: Amy Acton,Barack Obama,Sherrod Brown Democrats are eyeing the Senate and gubernatorial races as key pickup opportunities given the headwinds facing Republicans. Amy Acton campaign slams Ramaswamy over controversial ad featuring estranged mother In his remarks, Obama delivered a scathing rebuke of the Trump administration on a variety of issues — from the economy to immigration to the war in Iran. Regarding the GOP candidate for governor, Obama called Ramaswamy "thirsty" for attention. Sue Ogrocki/AP Photo - PHOTO: Election 2026 Ohio Senate "Vivek's own supporters know it's all about what's in it for him," Obama said. "We all know that guy, you know, who ... just wants to get attention no matter what, willing to do anything. And in recent days, we've seen there is no line he will not cross, no low he will not sink to." Obama emphasized what he called a "moral component" to this election and said that "basic decency" is missing from the current public discourse. ABC News' Diana Paulsen contributed to this report. articles.title: 12 people shot, including children, after Florida A&M homecoming game
articles.summary: At least 12 people, half of them juveniles and the youngest just 11 years old, were injured in a mass shooting near FAMU’s Bragg Memorial Stadium Saturday night amid homecoming weekend. Tallahassee Police Chief Lawrence Revell said 11 people suffered gunshot wounds. Three victims were seriously injured, including one in critical condition, while eight were stable. A FAMU student was among the injured. Police said preliminary information indicates an altercation occurred between individuals before the shooting, which Revell called an "isolated incident." The latest: FAMU homecoming ends with one of city's worst mass shootings; six victims still hospitalized Midnight update: At least 12 injured in Perry Street shooting; youngest victim is 11 At least 12 people were injured, including six juveniles, in the shooting near FAMU’s Bragg Memorial Stadium Saturday night, Tallahassee Police Chief Lawrence Revell said at a late-night press conference. “I stand before you tonight devastated,” Revell said. Eleven of the victims suffered gunshot wounds. Six victims are adults and six are juveniles, with the youngest just 11 years old, Revell said. A twelfth victim is the grandmother of one of the victims who was injured fleeing from the scene. He said one of the victims is a FAMU student. Three victims suffered serious injuries and one was in critical condition. Eight were in stable condition. He spoke directly to the victims and their families: "We hurt with you, and we will continue to get you the answers you so desperately want." The shooting occurred just before 8 p.m. near Perry and Manatee streets. Preliminary information indicates an altercation occurred between individuals before the shooting, Revell said. No one has been arrested at this time. Revell said investigators believe this was an "isolated incident between two or three individuals and nothing more than that." He asked anyone who saw anything or knows anything to come forward with information. Anyone with information is asked to call TPD at 850-891-4200 or Crime Solvers at 850-574-TIPS. More information will be released as it becomes available. "My message to the community is this... No family should have to experience this kind of violence, this kind of fear, this kind of heartbreak," he said. Revell took a moment to recognize "some of the heroic efforts" of first responders. "We had officers who were picking up victims and carrying them in their arms to transport because they couldn't get through the mass of people," he said. While choking up, he said it's critical for crowds to disperse so officers can get to victims. "Without hesitation they ran into the middle of this, still not knowing where the shooters were, still not knowing how many victims they had. They ran into the middle of this and put themselves in harms way." After midnight, Tallahassee Mayor John Dailey posted on x that “this is a truly horrific and heartbreaking tragedy.” “Tonight and in the days ahead, the FAMU family is not alone,” he wrote. “Our entire community stands with you.” 11:22 p.m. TPD and FAMU to hold press conference The Tallahassee Police Department and Florida A&M University Police Department will hold a press conference at 11:30 p.m. Saturday to provide updates on the Perry Street incident. The briefing will be held on FAMU’s campus at 1845 Althea Gibson Way. The announcement comes as authorities continue investigating the shooting near Bragg Memorial Stadium. Police previously said there were victims, but the number of people injured and the extent of their injuries remained unknown. The Tallahassee Democrat livestreamed it here. 11:10 p.m. FAMU issues statement: 'Our hearts go out to the victims and all those affected' At about 11 p.m., Florida A&M University issued a statement on the shooting through a Sachs Media representative sharing its condolences and saying the "campus remains safe." “The University is aware of an incident that occurred near campus on Perry Street on the evening of October 24. The Tallahassee Police Department is on the scene and actively investigating the situation." “Our hearts go out to the victims and all those affected by this tragic incident. While the campus remains safe, individuals are encouraged to avoid the area to allow law enforcement to conduct its investigation." “The safety and security of our students, faculty, and staff remain our highest priority. We are closely monitoring the situation and will share additional updates as more information becomes available. Anyone who has information about the situation is encouraged to contact the Tallahassee Police Department.” Anyone with information is asked to call TPD at 850-891-4200 or Crime Solvers at 850-574-TIPS. More information will be released as it becomes available. 10:30 p.m.: Social media videos show scenes of chaos Video of the shooting and its aftermath are circulating on social media. One video viewed by tens of thousands of people on Facebook shows police carrying a victim through a parking lot on a cloth stretcher. Another shows officers giving medical attention to a person on the ground by flashlight as people shout all around. Still another shows a swarm of police in all directions managing a crowd of bystanders. Trash litters the scene from where people fled in panic as bystanders talk about someone being hit in the head and another being shot in the back. "Everybody ran; everybody cleared off," a person can be heard saying. People also began coming to grips with the magnitude of the shooting on social media. "I can only imagine the level of panic and chaos that an incident of this magnitude may have caused. Beyond those directly affected by the shooting, my concern is that hundreds, perhaps even thousands, of people may have rushed to safety, potentially creating dangerous crowd surges and resulting in additional injuries," a pastor wrote on FAMU's Facebook page. "I sincerely pray that the number of injuries is minimal and that everyone affected is safe." ▶ Did you witness the shooting or its aftermath? Share your stories, photos or videos with us at news@tallahassee.com . Others took to social media to say their friends, family and loved ones were safe. "Praying for our kids because what I just witnessed at 7:50pm was unbelievable. My 1st and last homecoming. On God! My kids and their friends were crying and I'm trying to pull other people kids to safety," a witness wrote on Facebook. "This could have been any of our babies." A video taken earlier in the day before the gunfire showed massive crowds walking along Perry Street amid the homecoming festivities. 10:05 p.m. update: FSU issues alert to students: 'As a precaution,' stay indoors At 10 p.m., Florida State University issued an "Emergency Message for the Florida State University Tallahassee Campus" with the extraordinary advice to avoid going outside on a weekend evening. "Florida State University is aware of reports of an off-campus shooting near Bragg Stadium on the FAMU campus in Tallahassee earlier this evening (Sat. Oct 24). At this time, there is no indication that members of the FSU community were involved. As a precaution, students, faculty and staff in the Tallahassee area are advised to remain indoors this evening and stay alert. The university will provide additional information as appropriate." This is an Emergency Message for the Florida State University Tallahassee Campus. Florida State University is aware of reports of an off-campus shooting near Bragg Stadium on the FAMU campus in Tallahassee earlier this evening (Sat. Oct 24). At this t https://t.co/M1KzwIWsgV — FSU Alert (@FSUAlert) October 25, 2026 10 p.m.: TPD says scene is secure; no word on victims Alicia Hill with the Tallahassee Police Department told the Tallahassee Democrat at 9:45 p.m. that the scene was secure. She had not additional information about the number of victims or extent of injuries. She also could not say specifically where the gunfire occurred on Perry Street. TPD's online crime tracking map notes an 8:02 p.m. call to "Assist Other Agencies" at Perry and Manatee Streets, which is an intersection next to Bragg Stadium. FAMU posted at about 10 p.m. "TPD is investigating a shooting on Perry Street. The number of victims and extent of injuries are unknown. Please avoid the area while officers investigate." 9:15 p.m. UPDATE: TPD reports shooting on Perry Street with victims after FAMU issues 'shelter in place alert' The Tallahassee Police Department (TPD) posted on social media that it "is currently investigating a shooting on Perry Street. At this time, the number of victims and the extent of their injuries are unknown." "Community members are encouraged to avoid the area while officers conduct their investigation," the post on social media said. The news broke during a busy Florida A&M homecoming weekend and shortly after the Rattlers lost their homecoming game to Arkansas-Pine Bluff. The university sent out a campus safety alert at 8:40 p.m. to "shelter in place" and avoid the area near Bragg Stadium. TPD spokesperson Alicia Hill was heading to the scene but had no additional information other than to say "there certainly are victims." Hill said TPD was closing down Perry Street, and she said the agency would provide more updates when information was available. As news of the shooting spread, people who were on Perry Street began to post on social media what they saw. "Perry St was wild tonight. Running, falling, ducking and hiding," one person wrote. "They literally just shot these ppl in front of me," another person wrote. "Yall please pray for they families." A Tallahassee Democrat photojournalist said she heard a lot of sirens coming from multiple directions at about 8:15 p.m. She heard fire engines heading over probably 7-10 minutes later, and flying above were multiple police drones overhead headed toward Bragg. ORIGINAL STORY Florida A&M University issued a public safety alert Saturday night warning people to avoid the area around Bragg Memorial Stadium because of police activity. “FAMU Alert: Police activity near Bragg Stadium and perry street. Avoid the area or shelter in place if nearby,” the university said in the social media alert. The alert was posted at about 8:40 p.m., shortly after FAMU’s homecoming football loss. FAMU Alert: Police activity near Bragg Stadium and perry street . Avoid the area or shelter in place if nearby. — Florida A&M University (@FAMU_1887) October 25, 2026 The university did not immediately provide details about what prompted the police response or whether anyone had been injured. A Tallahassee Police Department Watch commander was not immediately available. People near Bragg Stadium and Perry Street were advised either to avoid the area or shelter in place. This is a developing story. Check back for updates. articles.title: 'Weaponizing the law': California AG slams DOJ's attack on alleged noncitizen voting
articles.summary: People cast their ballots at St Mary's Episcopal church during the first day of early voting in Los Angeles, California, on Saturday. Photograph: Chris Torres/EPA California’s attorney general on Saturday rebuked the Trump administration’s efforts to quash alleged noncitizen voting, calling it “politicizing and weaponizing the law”. Rob Bonta, the state’s attorney general, said the justice department acted at Donald Trump’s direction. “It is once again the United States Department of Justice politicizing and weaponizing the law to attack its enemies, and it is completely improper,” he told MS Now. Less than two weeks before the midterms, federal prosecutors called upon California election officials to verify within 48 hours a list of about 20,000 ballots belonging to suspected noncitizens. Noncitizen voting is extremely rare , but in the run-up to the midterm elections, the justice department has ramped up prosecutions of people accused of illegally voting while not holding US citizenship. California’s election personnel have raised concern that the administration’s directive could disenfranchise citizens. Los Angeles officials said this week a “high percentage” of the individuals on the list were born in the United States. “Trump’s DOJ is so desperate to invent ‘widespread voter fraud,’ it sent California counties lists of people who NEVER voted – and voters from the WRONG COUNTY. Absolute clown show!” California’s governor Gavin Newsom posted on social media . “Voter intimidation has no place in our democracy,” Pete Aguilar, a congressman representing south-west San Bernardino county, said in a social media post . The federal government’s oversight attempts come amid a national Republican effort to crack down on alleged voter fraud, particularly any cases among undocumented immigrants. “We are asking each county election official to commit to working with us by providing the necessary information for DHS to quickly verify citizenship status. With their help, we can ensure the most secure election in California history,” the justice department said. Bonta, the California attorney general, has raised questions about the evidence behind the suspected noncitizen ballots. “All they provided was a list of people and nothing about why they’re purportedly ineligible. If they have such information, we would be happy to review it, but they’ve provided none,” Bonta said at a recent press conference. The DoJ also charged 28 foreign nationals recently, accusing them of fraudulently registering to vote. “Today’s arrests prove what we have been saying,” Bill Essayli, first assistant US attorney, said in a statement. “California is mailing ballots to noncitizens, and they are refusing to comply with federal law, which makes it a crime for noncitizens to vote. The voting rights of American citizens must be protected.” The defendants are lawful permanent residents, who have legal status in the US but are not citizens authorized to vote. Some state officials took no action on Friday’s letters, citing the fast-approaching election, which spurred a legal battle with the justice department. An appeals court is set to hear the matter on Tuesday. articles.title: About 1,300 clergy abuse survivors approve $800 million deal with New York archdiocese
articles.summary: The Archdiocese of New York and attorneys for about 1,300 parishioners who said they were sexually abused by clergy have agreed to an $800 million settlement of their legal claims, the second-largest involving a Catholic archdiocese in the U.S. Archbishop Ronald Hicks sent an email Saturday to clergy confirming the settlement after attorneys for the survivors of alleged abuse announced it. Hicks said the agreement will not be final until the parties sign it, an action scheduled for the week of Nov. 6. The only larger settlement over sexual abuse claims in the U.S. was by the Archdiocese of Los Angeles, which agreed in 2024 to pay $880 million to 1,000 abuse victims, in addition to $740 million in claims it had paid previously. In June, the Archdiocese of San Francisco agreed to a $395 million settlement over about 500 lawsuits filed over clergy abuse, and in December 2025, a federal judge approved a settlement in which the Archdiocese of New Orleans agreed to pay at least $230 million to abuse victims. The agreement with the New York archdiocese would end more than seven years of lawsuits. The parties agreed to a framework for an agreement in May that required everyone who filed a claim to sign off. “The unanimous agreement of survivors who filed claims against the Archdiocese of New York marks a powerful moment in the pursuit of justice,” Jeff Anderson, an attorney representing people who filed more than 1,000 of claims against the Catholic Church in New York state, said in a statement. “Through their courage, sacrifice, and determination, survivors have helped bring about a reckoning and a meaningful step toward accountability.” The Archiocese of New York covers the city's boroughs of the Bronx, Manhattan and Staten Island as well as seven counties to the north of New York City and is home to about 300 churches, more than 150 parochial schools and 2.5 million Catholics. In his email to clergy, Hicks said that if church members ask about the settlement, “please let them know that much progress has been made.” “We are on the verge of being able to, please God, bring some measure of healing and reconciliation to all victim-survivors,” he wrote. “This agreement will also allow the archdiocese to turn its full attention once again to its mission of preaching the Gospel, healing the sick, caring for the poor and needy, welcoming the stranger, and educating our children.” A New York law enacted in 2019 allows survivors of child sexual abuse to file lawsuits against their abusers and institutions that shielded them until they turn 55. People who had already had turned 55 when the law was enacted also were given until August 2021 to file lawsuits, no matter when the alleged abuse occurred. “This is an extraordinary achievement for the survivors,” said Trusha Goffe, an attorney in Anderson’s firm. "The survivors remined resolute through years of litigation to reach this monumental settlement.” This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/articles/yorks-archdiocese-survivors-clergy-abuse-233516942.html

articles.title: Brazil's tight runoff tests Trump officials' bid to bring Bolsonaros back to power
articles.summary: By Gabriel Stargardter SAO PAULO, Oct 24 (Reuters) - Two US State Department officials led a campaign to restore the right-wing Bolsonaro clan to power in Brazil and successfully pushed for sanctions aimed at tilting the election in their favor, according to 10 current and former US officials with direct knowledge of the matter. Their plan faces a reckoning on Sunday, when Senator Flavio Bolsonaro faces leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in a tight run-off. Lula has warned Washington against encroaching on Brazil's sovereignty and accused his opponent of plotting with the Trump administration. The two officials were Darren Beattie, a Senior Advisor ‌for Western Hemisphere Affairs who oversees Brazil policy, and Ricardo Pita, another senior advisor promoted this year to Deputy Assistant Secretary for North America. The details of their campaign to return the Bolsonaros to power haven't been previously reported. Beattie and Pita, both political appointees, operated with wide latitude to manage Washington's relationship with the ‌second most-populous country in the Americas, the people said. In the months before election campaigning began, they instructed US diplomats in Brazil that it was US policy to restore former President Jair Bolsonaro as Brazil’s leader – even though he had been disqualified from office for plotting a coup in 2022, when he lost the presidential election to Lula, three of the people said. After Bolsonaro received a 27-year sentence in September 2025, the two men pivoted to ​supporting the candidacy of his son, right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the three sources said. Beattie and Pita told embassy staff not to interact with other conservative presidential contenders who could challenge the younger Bolsonaro, they said. Since last year, the two men have successfully advocated for punitive US government measures on Brazil designed to weaken Lula and boost the Bolsonaros, the 10 people told Reuters. The policies included designating Brazilian gangs as terrorist groups and imposing US sanctions against the Brazilian Supreme Court Justice who was spearheading the investigation into Jair Bolsonaro. Reuters could not determine the extent to which the two men were acting on orders from the White House or Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Trump, a vocal defender of Bolsonaro since his election defeat in 2022, hasn’t publicly endorsed any candidate. The White House declined to comment and referred questions to the State Department. State Department Spokesman Tommy Pigott didn't answer questions about specific measures and directives involving Beattie and Pita but said in a statement: "All actions taken by the United States against narco-traffickers and to protect free speech are to defend the rights and lives of the American people. The Brazilian people have the right to ‌choose their leaders through free and fair elections." Lula’s office did not respond to comment requests. Orna Blum, one of the officials who ⁠spoke to Reuters about Beattie and Pita’s efforts, led the State Department's Brazil and Southern Cone office until retiring last year over her opposition to the Trump administration. Washington "has every right to pursue its economic and strategic interests," she said. "But when American foreign policy instruments are used to pressure another democracy over the legal fate of a political ally, the line between diplomacy and political intervention has been crossed." SANCTIONS ON A SUPREME COURT JUSTICE Beattie is a former White House speechwriter fired in 2018 after addressing an event frequented by white nationalists. He’s also the architect of "free speech ⁠diplomacy," a policy advocated by Trump allies that seeks to punish nations they accuse of censoring right-wing speech by US citizens, companies and global right-wing allies. The United States has accused Brazil Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes of violating free speech rights by jailing Brazilians for political social-media posts and by censoring content of US social-media companies. Moraes has argued he was ridding social media of fake news that undermined public faith in Brazil's democratic institutions. Moraes did not respond to a comment request. Pita, a conservative Venezuelan-American, is among many in Rubio's orbit who view Lula as a threat to US interests in Latin America. Rubio has been a key leader in the administration’s aggressive policy in the region, which has included an invasion of Venezuela to oust its president, an oil blockade of Cuba, and military attacks ​on suspected ​drug boats from Latin America. Beattie and Pita were drawn to the Bolsonaro family’s right-wing politics, their antipathy towards Lula, and the idea that Jair Bolsonaro was a victim of abuses by Brazil's Supreme Court. Like ​Trump in the 2020 US election, Bolsonaro refused to concede he lost Brazil’s 2022 presidential vote, triggering riots by supporters who stormed government ‌buildings. The Supreme Court convicted him in September 2025 of plotting a coup to remain in power. Before the conviction, in early 2025, the Bolsonaros were aggressively lobbying Washington for sanctions under the Global Magnitsky Human Rights Accountability Act against Moraes, who had led criminal investigations into Jair Bolsonaro. The act is a 2016 federal law allowing US sanctions against foreign individuals responsible for human-rights abuses or severe corruption. Around April 2025, Jair Bolsonaro’s younger son, Eduardo, visited Beattie in his State Department office in Washington DC, according to two former US officials. Eduardo Bolsonaro had been making the public case for Magnitsky sanctions against Moraes since at least 2024, and in March 2025 he said in a livestream that it was "practically certain" the Trump administration would do so. Eduardo Bolsonaro did not respond to requests for comment. Beattie made calls to the US Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control to appeal for Magnitsky sanctions against Moraes, said a former US official with direct knowledge of the matter. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, whose department administers Magnitsky sanctions through OFAC, offered no opposition, the former official said. The US announced Magnitsky sanctions against Moraes in July 2025, citing his alleged violations of free-speech rights by censoring anti-government social-media posts. A Treasury official said Bessent and Rubio are "fully aligned on the administration’s foreign policy." TERRORIST DESIGNATIONS The Bolsonaro family was also pushing for Washington to designate Brazil's top gangs – the Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC) and Comando Vermelho (CV) – as terrorist organizations. They believed such a designation would hurt Lula, ‌who some opponents have criticized for failing to control crime. Eduardo Bolsonaro had become friends with Pita through US conservative circles, and both supported the effort to designate the gangs as terrorist groups. In May 2025, ​Pita joined a US delegation that visited Jair Bolsonaro at his residence in Brasilia as he awaited his trial, according to public announcements at the time. Also in the group: David Gamble, the State Department’s top sanctions ​official at the time. Back in Washington, Pita asked State sanctions officials to explore how terrorist designations like those announced against Mexican cartels in February 2025 could be used ​in Brazil, one former official said. Nearly a year later, in May 2026 – after Pita was promoted to a new job that pulled him out of Brazil affairs – presidential contender Flavio Bolsonaro met with Beattie and Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau in Washington to discuss "the urgency of designating the ‌PCC and the Comando Vermelho as foreign terrorist organizations," according to an X post by right-wing influencer Paulo Figueiredo that included ​photos of the attendees. The State Department announced the designation the following day. Reuters could not determine the ​extent of Pita or Beattie’s influence in securing the final decision. BACKFIRES AND SETBACKS In July 2025, Washington also announced a series of other measures against Brazil, including the revocations of eight Supreme Court justices' visas and 50% tariffs on Brazilian goods, citing the "persecution" of Jair Bolsonaro. Reuters could not determine what, if any, role Beattie or Pita played in the additional measures. But if they were intended to undermine Lula, many of them backfired, according to political analysts in Brazil. Measures targeting the court did nothing to stop it from proceeding with Bolsonaro's trial, while the tariffs boosted the Lula government's poll numbers, the analysts said. Major US and Brazilian firms reliant on bilateral trade – including ​meatpacking giant JBS - controlled by Brazilian billionaires Wesley and Joesley Batista – also pushed back on the tariffs, which Washington eventually watered down. Beattie ‌and Pita’s campaign also hit setbacks. Without an official explanation from the Treasury Department, the US removed Justice Moraes from the Magnitsky sanctions list in December, and in March Brazil barred Beattie from entering the country to visit Bolsonaro in prison. Mario Braga, a Latin America analyst at risk intelligence firm RANE, ​said Trump may have decided to withhold a public endorsement of Bolsonaro to avoid being seen as meddling in Brazil's election – a perception that could boost Lula’s popularity. Still, after Flavio Bolsonaro narrowly outperformed Lula in the first-round election earlier this month, Trump called it a big victory. "Close, but a very, very ​big victory," he told reporters. "Amazing, actually." (Reporting by Gabriel StargardterAdditional reporting by Gram Slattery in Washington, Luciana Magalhaes in Sao Paulo, Lisandra Paraguassu in Brasilia Editing by Brad Haynes and Richard Valdmanis) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/inside-trump-administration-campaign-return-214506018.html

articles.title: Musk says he was behind Starlink disruptions, claiming Ukraine service violations
articles.summary: KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Elon Musk said on Saturday that his company SpaceX had throttled the Starlink satellite internet service in Ukraine, disrupting operations that the country relies on to defend itself against Russia. Musk's admission on social media came after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Ukraine’s access to Starlink and Starshield satellite links has been restored to the speeds it had before restrictions that disrupted front-line operations for more than a week. Questions have persisted since last week about who ordered the interruptions to the Musk-made satellite internet system that Kyiv has relied on for years to counter Moscow’s attacks . “The speeds are now where they need to be,” Zelenskyy wrote on X, adding that restoration began overnight and were sufficient by Saturday morning, improving front-line logistics and defense against Russian jet-powered Shahed drones. Musk admits he was behind Starlink’s speed restriction After Ukraine said the services had been restored, Elon Musk spoke out on the speed restrictions that began last week. In a post Saturday on X, Musk acknowledged that his company SpaceX throttled the Starlink satellite internet service. “Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be,” Musk wrote. “Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week.” But he maintained that the U.S. government controlled whatever changes happened with Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink that is the backbone of Ukraine’s drone operations and communication. He also defended the role of SpaceX in bolstering Ukraine’s defenses since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Restrictions imposed last week on Starshield alarmed the country’s military and government officials, with commanders reporting lost drones and disrupted missions. The restoration follows a new U.S. diplomatic push to end the war. Russia agreed Wednesday to resume three-way negotiations with Washington and Kyiv next month. On Friday, Kyiv and Moscow also agreed to a localized ceasefire brokered by first lady Melania Trump around Oleshky , a war-ravaged, Russian-occupied town in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region. Restriction led to tensions between Ukraine and the US The episode added to tensions between Kyiv and Washington, a relationship already strained by President Donald Trump’s reported deal with Moscow on Russian diesel imports, which Ukraine viewed as a betrayal. Ukraine's Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara credited “direct dialogue” and Zelenskyy’s diplomacy with Washington, adding that the outcome mattered most “for our front, for the military, the work of drones, logistics and communications.” Trump has maintained that he didn’t make the call, while also saying Musk should not be blamed. Vice President JD Vance has hinted at White House coordination with Musk, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth have denied any administration involvement. Russia and Ukraine have continued to target each other Meanwhile, a man was killed and two others wounded in a missile attack on the city of Lozova in Ukraine's Kharkiv region, local officials said Saturday. Moscow-installed authorities in cities across Russia-occupied Crimea reported power blackouts Saturday following overnight Ukrainian attacks. Ukraine’s General Staff said Saturday that its forces hit a chemical plant in the Russian city of Tolyatti, which produces materials used in rocket fuel. Tolyatti Mayor Ilya Sukhikh said the overnight attack damaged industrial facilities in the city. Ukrainian forces also hit an electronics plant in the city of Oryol, Ukraine’s General Staff confirmed Saturday. Local officials in Oryol said Saturday that three people were killed in Friday’s attack. The General Staff said the plant makes components for the cruise and ballistic missiles Russia fires at Ukrainian cities. Ukrainian drones also reached Russia’s Omsk region in western Siberia, more than 2,000 kilometers (1,242 miles) from the border with Ukraine. Omsk regional Gov. Vitaly Khotsenko said drones “reached a northern industrial hub.” Online retailer Ozon said Saturday that its logistics center in Omsk has been attacked by a drone, but there were no casualties. Ozon is a competitor to Wildberries, whose facilities Ukraine has also targeted. ___ Morton reported from London. ___ Follow the AP’s coverage of the war in Ukraine at https://apnews.com/hub/russia-ukraine This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/articles/ukraine-says-starlink-speed-limits-104548676.html

articles.title: Signs point to renewed major U.S. military operations against Iran
articles.summary: A photo released by the US Navy shows an F/A-18 Super Hornet launching from the flight deck of the USS George Washington as it operates in the Middle East on September 9, 2026 (-) The United States appears to be preparing to resume large-scale strikes against Iran, but there is unlikely to be a military solution for either side in the devastating conflict, experts say. Washington and Tehran's forces have settled into a pattern of strikes on commercial ships, with the United States seeking to enforce a blockade of Iran's ports and the Islamic republic trying to exert control over the key Strait of Hormuz waterway. Neither country has engaged in major attacks on land-based targets since early September, but that may soon change. "I'm banking now on the likelihood of strikes shortly after the midterms," said Suzanne Maloney, director of the foreign policy program at the Brookings Institution, referring to November 3 elections in the United States. She pointed to potential signs including the movement of additional US military assets and troops to the Middle East, warnings issued to Americans in the region, and a high alert status for Israeli forces. Additionally, President Donald Trump "came out publicly and said that he wouldn't strike before the midterms," and "it wouldn't seem to help him at the polls to do so," Maloney said. The US-Israeli war against Iran is largely unpopular in the United States, especially because it has sharply driven up fuel prices, and is likely to be a drag on Trump's Republican Party in the key vote. "Fundamentally, the situation isn't sustainable in its current state," Maloney said, noting that the US blockade is "creating greater pain for the Iranians," while Washington has a large number of naval assets tied up in enforcing it. Trump said Friday that "we may do another little Epic Fury" -- the name for the US operation against Iran that was launched in late February -- if Tehran does not make a deal, but gave no indication on timing. - 'Impossible to predict' - Jason Campbell, a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute, said there have "certainly been recent signs that renewed strikes may be in the offing," or that "the US is expecting strikes carried out by Iran" or their Houthi allies in Yemen. He noted the planned deployment of the USS Theodore Roosevelt to the Middle East -- which could at least temporarily bring the number of carrier strike groups there to three -- as well as the decision to dispatch another Marine Expeditionary Unit to the region. Campbell also said Israeli warplanes recently carried out a "show of force" mimicking previous strikes on Iran, and noted that US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had met with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Israel. However, "timing here is impossible to predict," he said of renewed strikes, while noting that "this is admittedly an expansive set of actions to take if the intent is to simply pressure Iran to the negotiating table." Campbell said Trump's options are more limited than they were earlier in the conflict, with damage to US bases in the region having made any potential ground operation more difficult. "At this point, there is no safe place to stage the thousands (in some scenarios tens of thousands) of forces that would be required for such an operation," he said. Maloney meanwhile said that "most of the conventional military sites (in Iran) have already been heavily degraded" by previous strikes, meaning any new campaign will likely "entail more strikes on civilian infrastructure and targets that impact the Iranian population." But that -- or any type of military action -- is unlikely to bring about a resolution to the conflict. "From the start... this has been a war that can't be ended with further escalation on either side," Maloney said. Campbell agreed, saying: "I do not see how renewed strikes on Iran akin to the first fifty days of the war will move the strategic needle for the Iranian regime." "They have demonstrated a willingness to absorb a significant amount of physical pain and even some alterations to targeting that includes key mixed or even civilian infrastructure will not significantly change this," he added. wd/sms This article originally appeared on AFP at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/signs-point-renewed-major-us-175157103.html

articles.title: 价格打折，哪些股票超跌了？
articles.summary: 双十一，股市也开启了“打折促销”。近期市场快速调整，创业板指从4372点回落到2700点以下，科创综指来到1300附近。不少前期热门股票大幅回撤，以历史高点为参照，中际旭创、新易盛、东山精密等热门股价格已跌至约四折。 尽管10月23日市场明显反弹，但科技成长板块此前的调整幅度已经不小，也引发了市场对科技股是否会重演周期股大幅波动的担忧。 股票毕竟不是普通商品，价格打折不等于估值便宜。 从交易层面看，下跌太快，股价反而可能出现反弹。但这类交易性反弹，并不是我们要讨论的“超跌”。 我们所说“超跌”是基于完整盈利周期基础上的估值便宜。 投资者在这个价格上购买股票，可能会输掉一些时间，但不会丧失本金。 为此，我们拿出光伏，锂电的龙头，跟光通信龙头进行比较。光伏和锂电都有完整的周期可以参考。 通过选取隆基绿能、宁德时代和中际旭创作为典型案例，比较不同景气阶段下的盈利和估值变化，观察经历大幅调整后，当前股价是否已经出现估值超跌。 看PE、PB的历史分位，不能判断估值 股价大幅调整后，市场通常把PE、PB放到历史的维度里去比较 ：当前低于历史多少分位，就说股票有多便宜。 例如，仅看原始PE的分布，宁德时代截至今年9月30日，15.85倍的pe低于此前五年20个季度的全部观测值；中际旭创当前32倍估值处于历史40%分位水平。单看历史估值，宁德时代似乎已经比较便宜，中际旭创也不算贵。 但问题是，这一估值背后所对应的盈利并不相同。 对于景气波动较大的公司，历史估值分位未必能反映真实的估值水平。仅是用历史分位，很难判断在周期中，是否真的“超跌”。 行业景气高低点，企业盈利水平差异明显 周期股在景气高点和低谷的盈利差异往往很大。即期估值容易受到利润波动的影响。 把三家公司利润放在一起来进行对比，通过年末EPS和ROE的观察，对周期差异就有更直观的感觉。 隆基2022年末ROE还有23.8%，2026年二季度却降至-15.5%，EPS也转为负数；中际旭创2021年末ROE只有7.6%，2026年二季度已超过51%，EPS从约1元增至13.4元；宁德时代的EPS则从2021年末约4.3元增加到2026年二季度约17.1元。 景气高点，利润增长会压低PE；景气低谷，利润收缩甚至亏损，又会使PE大幅抬升或失去参考意义。这就是单看即期PE容易踩的“坑”。 因此，仅凭PE、PB的历史分位，难以准确判断股价是否超跌。 我们尝试以历史稳态ROE为基准，还原企业在正常盈利水平下的估值，进一步观察当前股价是否具备安全边际。 估值是否合理，需要考虑完整的景气周期 经历大幅调整后， 优质公司的股价是否已经跌至具有吸引力的位置，需要从完整的行业景气周期出发，以正常盈利水平为参照。 我们采用历史ROE中位数作为稳态盈利水平，据此测算修正后的EPS和PE，观察企业在正常盈利能力下的历史估值区间，进而判断当前股价是否具备估值安全边际。 三家公司，三个答案 我们以三家公司各自的盈利周期起始日为起点，选取此后26个季度的ROE（TTM）中位数作为稳态盈利参考，并据此修正历史EPS和PE。 这样剔除不同景气阶段盈利波动对PE的影响，在相对统一的盈利水平下，观察市场过去给予企业的估值是否合理。 隆基绿能：便宜的前提，是先把利润赚回来 隆基的历史样本为2016Q1—2022Q2。26个季度的ROE中位数为19.53%，对应的标准化PE中位数为26.43倍。 问题是，隆基目前仍在亏损，负PE已经没法正常比较。按2026Q3的11.21元股价倒推：如果未来ROE恢复到约7.22%，对应PE为26.43倍；如果恢复到历史中位数19.53%，对应PE约9.76倍。 对隆基来说，能不能恢复盈利、能恢复到什么水平，比股价跌了多少更重要。 宁德时代：把盈利调回常态后，估值仍偏低 宁德的历史样本为2018Q2—2024Q3。ROE中位数为13.48%，标准化PE中位数为49.12倍，历史25%—75%区间为36.79—81.43倍。 2026Q3，宁德时代PE为15.85倍。把当期ROE折回13.48%后，修正PE约26.64倍，仍低于历史区间下沿，处在历史约3.8%分位。 换句话说，宁德的低PE并不只是当下盈利较高造成的。即使用历史中位数ROE来算，估值相对过去仍然偏低，具备一定的历史估值吸引力。 中际旭创：PE不高，不代表安全垫已经很厚 中际的历史样本为2020Q1—2026Q2。ROE中位数为10.73%，标准化PE中位数为61.95倍。 只看当前32倍PE，它处在原始PE历史约34.6%分位，处于较低分位水平。但如果用历史ROE中位数来折算，当前示意标准化PE约153倍，处于历史约84.6%分位，超过历史中间50%区间。 两种口径之所以差这么多，关键在于对高ROE能持续多久的判断。 如果未来ROE逐渐回到历史水平，当前价格在这套模型下没有明显的绝对吸引力；但如果AI光模块需求带来的高盈利能维持较长时间，用10.73%的历史ROE做假设又可能过于保守。 跌下来以后，究竟怎样才算便宜？ 三家公司给出了不同的答案：宁德时代在盈利还原至历史中枢后，估值仍处于历史较低分位；隆基绿能的估值吸引力取决于盈利修复；中际旭创则需要关注当前高ROE的持续性。 从跨周期估值角度看，判断股价是否超跌，不能仅依据股价回撤幅度或短期交易性反弹，更需要考察企业在稳态盈利水平下的估值位置。 若盈利回归常态后，估值仍明显偏高，说明当前价格对盈利回落的风险反映可能不足；若在相对保守的盈利假设下，估值仍处于历史低位，则可能具备一定的安全边际，但仍需结合基本面判断折价是否合理。 不过需要注意的是，历史中位数不能代替未来盈利预测，行业景气和公司竞争力也可能发生变化。但把价格与可持续的赚钱能力放在一起看，至少能避免把“跌得多”直接当成“够便宜”。 股价打了几折不重要。重要的是，利润回到正常水平以后，价格是否依然合理。 本文来源： 东吴证券陈李、葛晓媛 风险提示及免责条款 articles.title: AI势头回落并非牛熊分界
articles.summary: AI趋势回落并非熊市开端，非AI可能反而会面临更为有利的环境 1）产业趋势回落≠牛转熊。A股在过往存在比较广泛的“产业趋势回落=牛转熊”的思维，核心是过往的产业趋势（2006~2007年的工业与金融、2009年的地产与基建、2013~2015年的移动互联、2019~2021年的能源转型等）对其他经济部门带来广泛的拉动作用。而本轮AI产业的进展，至少在短期内对其他经济部门产生了不少挤出效应，包括导致了物料和资源价格暴涨、推动了债券市场供需紧张和长债利率大幅飙升、一定程度上挤出就业，财富效应的增长极为失衡，市场分化的程度历史罕见，甚至出现了所谓“硅基世界”和“碳基世界”的对立。这也意味着，过往“产业趋势行情结束=牛转熊”的经验可能并不适用于这轮AI硬件主导的行情，非AI的不少板块早已步入下行趋势，而AI只不过最后“补跌”。 2）AI短期内对其他部门产生了负外部性，若AI势头回落，一些非AI板块反而可能有转机。目前已经显性化的负外部性至少包含三类：第一，电子元器件、电力等基础生活物资的大幅涨价，抬高生产和生活成本，压抑其他领域需求，典型的如消费电子；第二，算力基础设施投建推动私人部门巨额债务融资，推升全球无风险利率，对所有高利率敏感性的需求产生冲击；第三，挤出就业，尤其是对于年轻人就业的影响，比如根据斯坦福与ADP就业数据库今年9月最新数据，自动化型AI使用占比最高职业组的22~25岁就业较2022年11月下降10.9%，最低组同期上升7.8%。这些因素引发了实体经济和市场的剧烈分化，但反过来看，如果AI投资的速度在未来有所放缓，非AI板块可能也不会面临如此负面的宏观环境，比如无风险利率出现大幅回落。事实上，从当前的美债定价来看，10年期美债利率的走向与北美AI硬件股的股价走势高度相关，如果未来出现持续性的回落，至少对海外的非AI部门需求可能产生促进。 估值收缩的进程今年已基本完成，行情宽度有望逐步拓展 1）AI的二阶导修正、非AI的估值收缩，都有望在今年基本完成。AI完成了第一波“二阶导”修正。与2021年底至2022年4月底的新能源行情调整类似，本轮AI同样是在产业景气仍在、增速预期转弱时提前下修估值。从估值收缩的视角出发，本轮AI硬件的估值压缩幅度已与2022年新能源第一轮调整相当。根据Wind数据，7月1日以来，电子与通信板块整体法PE（TTM）从74.0倍压缩至42.4倍，降幅42.8%；2022年新能源第一轮调整（2021年12月17日-2022年4月26日），电力设备及新能源板块市值下PE从51.2倍压缩至27.8倍，降幅45.7%。站在全球对比的视角下，A股非AI板块处于全球估值洼地。我们用中、美、日、韩四个市场的AI与非AI龙头篮子，以整体法测算PE（TTM）并进行跨市场对比。截至10月22日，A股是唯一一个AI相对非AI估值溢价仍高于历史中枢的市场：AI/非AI的PE倍数为4.4倍，处于2016年以来82%的分位，美、日、韩的这一倍数则分别回落至1%、17%、24%的分位。美、日非AI非金融龙头的PE分别为33.5倍和23.0倍，处于98%和95%的分位；A股非AI非金融龙头只有15.6倍，处于历史21%分位，消费、制造、医药龙头分别只处于12%、1%、3%的分位。当然，低估值源于疲弱的内需以及市场对非AI领域外需的潜在担忧（贸易摩擦、海外高利率、高油价等），有其合理性。但换个角度看，这种导致低估值的悲观，很大程度上源于今年的现实与年初市场期待的巨大割裂，投资者难以预料在“十五五”的第一年广义财政赤字会意外转为大幅负增长、市场从美联储降息预期转为加息预期、10年期美债利率创了2007年以来新高、中欧贸易摩擦突然升温、美伊战争爆发且持续快一年。这种落差，是导致不少非AI板块在今年业绩增长亮眼的情况下估值发生剧烈收缩的原因。当下，至少市场已经充分认知到了这些宏观负面因素，无论是海外利率还是国内政策，任何边际上超预期的变化可能都有助于改变当下A股相对于全球市场更为悲观的估值体系。 2）K型分化逐步收敛，行情宽度有望逐步拓展。对于AI侧，商业化空间增长焦虑还将继续约束AI投资单年度的绝对规模体量，同时加深市场对于未来“一阶导”拐点的警惕，AI对于非AI板块的虹吸很难再出现，同时考虑到主流机构资金仍然超配TMT板块，市场反弹过程中的持仓均衡化过程也将制约AI板块的弹性。我们看到，在本周市场止跌企稳的过程中，率先反弹的AI新技术是筹码出清相当彻底且机构持仓比例低的机器人板块，而非算力基建相关的板块。对非AI板块，当下几乎所有的负面因素都已经被市场所认知（即便可能并未完全定价），在经历一轮系统性调整后，低预期本身就是有利的条件。以出海板块为例，中欧贸易摩擦已经摆在台面上，未来每年的规则修订谈判和博弈可能是常态化的，企业最终还是会凭借强大的竞争优势适应；人民币在明年只要升值速度有所放缓，汇兑损失就会同比减少，就会带来净利润率的回升；美国中期选举后民主党如果控制国会，中东战争格局可能会有积极变化，所带来的油价影响可能边际上转弱；AI投资增速放缓，带来海外长端无风险利率回落，对非AI行业的需求抑制作用减弱。由于这些负面因素在今年已经被投资者系统性认知，只要后续有边际上的好转，对非AI板块本身也产生促进。 资金面的出清需要时间，PB-ROE 代表的稳健回报型策略可能更加占优 资金面快速恶化的过程大概率已接近尾声，在本周ETF明显放量的信号下，主动买盘开始谨慎流入市场，融资盘去杠杆的负向循环被阻断。截至10月21日，两市融资余额已回落至2.45万亿元，相对年内高点累计减少5600亿元，降幅18.6%，已回到去年11月下旬的水平，交易层面的降温更为明显，融资买入额占两市成交额的比例（MA5，下同）6月平均为9.86%，7月降至8.99%，9月为8.66%，10月以来进一步降至8.01%，10月16日读数7.84%，为2024年9月以来的最低值，低于“9.24”行情前约9%的水平。活跃私募的仓位同样回到低位，对中信证券渠道调研显示，样本活跃私募仓位8月7日当周以来持续回落，10月16日已降至67.5%，为2024年3月以来最低，较76.3%的历史中位数低8.8个百分点。虽然资金面指标已经回落到较低的位置，但彻底出清并开始持续改善仍然需要时间，这个阶段动量和景气策略会持续弱势，市场轮动速度加快，而以PB-ROE外代表的低估值质量型策略会更占优。目前有两类行业在明年满足这样的框架，一类是具备高股息率和稳健盈利增速的品种，如白电、纺织服装、食品调味、火电等，另一类是带有供给出清潜力逻辑的品种，如油运、快递物流、头部地产开发商、部分锂电材料、石化偏中游的环节等。 articles.title: SemiAnalysis创始人深度解析：AI投资还能撑多久？英伟达护城河还能守住吗？内存荒何时结束？
articles.summary: AI基础设施投资仍有增长空间，但融资成本上升、半导体供应链受限与自研芯片竞争加剧，正在共同考验这轮AI热潮的持续性。 在10月23日于美国举行的CASPA第35届年度大会上，SemiAnalysis创始人兼CEO Dylan Patel、Bernstein董事总经理兼高级分析师 Stacy Rasgon，以及Austin Lyons围绕半导体行业前景展开讨论，重点涉及AI基础设施投资、供应链瓶颈与芯片竞争格局。 Patel指出， 当前AI算力需求依然旺盛，但基板、内存等关键环节的产能约束，正在限制基础设施扩张。 与此同时，融资成本大幅攀升，缺乏长期客户订单的新兴云服务商越来越难以获得资金，AI投资能否持续推进，不仅取决于需求，也取决于项目的融资能力与回报。 对于英伟达，Rasgon认为，其产品性能提升仍能支撑较高售价，但云厂商自研芯片正在改变竞争格局。 随着Google TPU、亚马逊Trainium以及OpenAI等企业的自研芯片计划推进，英伟达即使继续增长，也可能面临市场份额和定价能力的双重压力。 内存市场则面临另一重考验：HBM需求旺盛、行业利润率处于高位，但厂商扩产可能在2028年后逐步改变供需关系。未来两年，融资能力、关键零部件供给与自研芯片的竞争，将成为影响AI基础设施扩张速度和产业链利润分配的关键变量。 华尔街见闻总结要点如下： AI投资仍有增长空间，但融资成本正成为重要约束。 HBM的特殊之处在于，其制造需要消耗更多晶圆资源。随着AI加速器需求增长，HBM扩产不仅要增加自身产能，也会影响其他DRAM产品的供给。短期内，产能分配与扩产速度难以迅速跟上需求；但随着新产能陆续投产，供需关系也可能发生逆转。 内存短缺何时结束，关键不在于某个固定日期，而在于新增产能何时开始超过需求增量。 如果扩产集中在2028年以后，而AI需求增速同时放缓，当前的高价格和高利润率就可能难以维持。 投资者需要关注HBM与DRAM扩产进度、先进封装和晶圆制造能力，以及云厂商资本开支的变化。在供给明显增加之前，内存仍可能制约AI算力交付；但在更长周期内，扩产也可能成为压低价格、侵蚀利润的因素。 英伟达护城河还能守住吗？性能优势面临自研芯片挑战 英伟达的核心优势，在于持续提升芯片性能，并通过软件生态和开发工具增强客户黏性。但随着云厂商越来越重视算力成本，其高售价也为自研芯片提供了发展空间。 但竞争对手正在加快追赶。 Patel的研究显示，英伟达在相关协处理器晶圆及HBM需求中的份额占比已开始下滑。 与此同时，Google TPU已向外部客户销售，亚马逊Trainium持续完善对PyTorch生态的支持，OpenAI和Anthropic也在推进自研芯片计划。 这些布局未必会立即取代英伟达，却能为大型客户提供替代方案，增强其议价能力。 对于拥有庞大算力需求的云厂商而言，自研芯片的吸引力不仅在于降低采购成本，也在于减少对单一供应商的依赖。 因此，英伟达面临的关键考验不是能否继续增长，而是能否持续以性能优势证明其价格溢价合理。即使AI市场整体扩大，英伟达的收入、市场份额与利润率也未必同步增长。 企业AI落地：购买Token比自建算力更现实 在企业应用端，三位分析师认为，大多数企业不会自行采购大量硬件运行私有模型，而是通过云服务购买Token，即调用云端AI推理能力，再与自有数据和业务流程结合。这与过去企业IT从自建基础设施转向云计算的趋势相似。
